full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the pre-emptor is directed against a judgment of affirmance in a proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

 3. The O.P. No. 1 traversing the material allegations made in the application contested the claim of the petition contending, inter alia, that the petitioner was fully aware of the sale when it took place. The application is eventually barred by limitation. It was further contended that the petitioner is not a co-sharer of the holding of the land and be Las no locus stand to make this application for preemption. The petitioner was a co-sharer of the superior Taluk. The other co-sharers created tenancy in favour of Shambhu Charan Misir in Mirash right and Shambhu Charan in his turn settled the suit land with Atul Chandra Das in raiyati interest and Atul was in possession of the disputed land as a raiyat under Shambhu Charan when he transferred his interest to Taiyabunnessa. The superior interest has already been acquired by State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The petitioner has no interest in the disputed land and the application filed by him is misconceived and not maintainable. 

 5. On appeal, the learned Subordinate Judge affirmed the decision of the learned Munsif on both the counts. The learned Subordinate Judge clearly found that "the present petitioner is not a co-sharer of the tenancy held by Atul Chandra Das as a raiyati holding. As such the petitioner has no locus stand to file this application for pre-emption and this application for pre-emption is not maintainable under the law." The learned Subordinate Judge further found that the application was barred by limitation. According to the learned Subordinate Judge "the petitioner was aware of the transfer made to Taiyabunncssa by Atul Chandra Das when it took place. So, I decide this point also against the petitioner and I find that the case is absolutely barred by limitation." 

 6. Mr. Salam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner contends that the petitioner is a co-sharer in the land. According to him after the acquisition of superior interest, the petitioner become a tenant in respect of the disputed lard along with other tenants including Atul Chandra Das. The learned Advocate submits that the property in suit being a tank is impartible in nature and as such the pre-emptor become a co-sharer in joint ownership and possession with ether tenants. Mr. Salary has Prefaced his contention by referring to the decision in the case of, Anwara Begunm Chowdhurani and Shamsul Huda Chowdhury Vs. Nur Jahan Begum and others reported in 27 DLR (Appellate Division) 109. There is no dispute with the proposition that after the notification issued under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the status of an under raiyat was upgraded to that of a tenant. There is also no dispute that with the acquisition of rent-receiving interests by the Government, all the intermediary interests disappeared and a person holding land under the landlord became a tenant holding land directly under the Government. These aspects of law have no direct reference to the question raised by the learned Advocate. The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act did not contemplate the merger of all the existing tenancies into one common tenancy and all the tenants under the different tenancies become co-sharers in such a tenancy. The facts of the instant case clearly indicate that the petitioner was a co-sharer of the Touzi No. 358 recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 1. There is no dispute that Hemanga Mohan Bardhan was a co-sharer in the said Khatian. No. 1. This Bardhan settled some land of the disputed tank in favour of Shambhu Charan Misir. The settlement obtained by Shambhu Charan constituted a tenancy distinct and separate from the holding recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 1. It further appears that Shambhu Charan settled the suit land in favour of Atul Chandra Das by a registered Kabuliyat Exhibit B dated 5. 9. 46 in raiyati right. Thus the raiyati right of Atul Chandra Das constituted a holding which was different from the holding of Shambhu Charan and the holding recorded C. S. Khatian No. 1. On an analysis of these facts, it transpires that the contention of Mr. Salain, leads to an absurd proposition of law. By no stretch of imagination it can be conceived that with the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act coming into force, all these three holdings merged into one holding and all the tenants in respect of these different holdings became co-sharers to one common holding, in other words a co-tenancy emerged. The effect of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is that the intermediary interests ceased to exist and the tenants who were holding as under-tenants became tenants directly under the Government. Mr. Salam, however, could not cite any authority in support of his proposition. He has, however, referred to the case of Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury and another Vs. Musammat Rezia Begum and another 16 DLR 77 to contend that Atul Chandra Das, Shambhu Charan and Bardhan became co-sharers with the petitioner. The principle laid down in the said case does not extend any Support to the view Mr. Salim has advanced. He has relied upon the following passage from the case of Brindaban Chandra: 

 "If a share or portion of a non-agricultural land is sold, then a person can be a co-sharer tenant, even if he is not a co-possessor (physical speaking) of the specified land, provided a co-tenancy is established in respect of land itself. The sharing of the tenancy in respect of land is the gist of the Section. The co-tenancy itself must appertain to the disputed land and not to any other land. This is the plain meaning of the words "co-sharer tenants of such land." The passage referred to and relied upon by Mr. Salam is of no assistance to him unless he succeeds in proving "that a co-tenancy is established in respect of the land itself" as observed earlier. The different holdings standing in the name of Atul, Shambhu Charan and the Bardhans with the petitioner did never constitute a co-tenancy. In the circumstances this decision is of no assistance of Mr. Salam. 

 7. Further, on the date of the transfer namely, 10-8-55 the petitioner was not a co-sharer in a tenancy in respect of the land. Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act cud not come in operation to invest a person with a right which was not available to him on the date of transfer. Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act makes no reference to any retrospective operation of the right of pre-emption. Thus, in any view of the matter whether the properly is partible or not, whether or not the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act made the petitioner a tenant in respect of the land held by him under khatian No. 1, the petitioner was not a co-sharer having a right of pre-emption under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

 10. Mr. Salam referring to a decision in the case of Mrs. Zohura Begum Vs. Rafiqul Kader 25 DLR 91 contended that "knowledge is something more than mere knowledge that a decree had been passed against him in a particular court in favour of particular person for a particular sum (or in respect of particular property) and not merely the knowledge, that decree has been passed by some Court against him." This reference does not help Mr. Salam to get over the hurdle of limitation. Knowledge is a fact and is referable to certain state of things representing a fact. Knowledge is not a mere information but something more. Knowledge pre-supposes a knower and a known. Knowledge is a knower-known relation, a product of interaction between the knowing self or subject and the object to be known. It is not a mere subjective state of mind or a simple objective representation but a conscious relation between the subjective mind and the objective phenomenon. A clear and definite perception of necessary particulars of a fact may be said to constitute "knowledge" which is in essence a question of fact to be determined in the facts and circumstances of each case. The information about the transfer by Atul Chandra Das in favour of Taiyabunnessa received from the plaint of Title Suit No. 109 of 1967 did not represent the material particulars to establish a relationship between the object namely the transfer and the knower namely, the petitioner. The particulars disclosed by the said plaint were not sufficient to enable the petitioner to make the application upon compliance of the requirements of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. More material particulars were necessary for the purpose. But the Courts below did not accept on evidence, the petitioner's alleged, facts constituting his knowledge. The learned courts below took into consideration the evidence adduced by the contending parties and on assessment of evidence concurrently found that the petitioner had knowledge of the transfer when it took place. On a careful consideration of the judgments of the courts below, it transpires that the finding as regards the knowledge of the transfer does not suffer form any imperfection. Further, the fact of possession, according to the courts below, indicated the knowledge of the petitioner. 

 For the reasons stated above, the contentions raised by Mr. Salam are of no substance and must consequently fail.
